title: The talbiyah
hook: here I am, O Allah, here I am, no partner have You

segments.voice: Yesterday, what ihram forbids, and your line: restraint is the dress. Did the habit you set down stay down? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

Somebody calls your name across a room. Before you've decided anything, before you know what they want, you answer. Here. Yes? I'm here. In the Qur'an, Ibrahim is told to make a call of his own. Pickthall's translation of surah twenty-two: "And proclaim unto mankind the Pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." A call goes out. And on the roads to Mecca, people answer it, out loud, over and over. Today, the answer.
screen: `SOMEONE CALLS YOUR NAME.` → `PROCLAIM THE PILGRIMAGE.` → `THEY WILL COME.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Abdullah ibn Umar reported the talbiyah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it's kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. In Arabic it begins: labbayk Allahumma labbayk. In English, roughly: here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am, You have no partner, here I am. Praise and blessing are Yours, and the dominion. You have no partner. That's all of it. A handful of short lines, said again and again. Second, the shape of the word labbayk. It isn't a request. It's a reply, the word for answering someone who has called you, here I am, at your service. The pilgrim isn't starting a conversation. The pilgrim is responding to one. Some readers connect that to Ibrahim's call in surah twenty-two: he proclaimed, and the pilgrims, generation after generation, are still answering. Third, the line that comes twice: no partner have You. In the middle of a journey full of crowds and rituals and holy places, the talbiyah keeps pointing past all of it, to one God alone. Fourth, the sound. A report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet saying that the angel Jibril came and told him to have his companions raise their voices with the talbiyah. So the roads, the buses, the airports and the tents carry it out loud, men's voices raised, women's usually lower. A pilgrim begins it on entering ihram and keeps it going for days. Yesterday's story ended with a man who died in ihram and would be raised still saying it. This is what he'd be saying. Here I am.
screen: `HERE I AM, O ALLAH, HERE I AM.` · `A REPLY, NOT A REQUEST.` · `NO PARTNER HAVE YOU.` · `RAISE YOUR VOICES.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it, or hear it. Settle, and breathe. If you're Muslim, or pray, you can say the talbiyah quietly in Arabic: labbayk Allahumma labbayk. Say it slowly, a few times, and notice that each line is an answer. If you're not, you can simply listen to the English words in your head, here I am, and notice what it would mean to answer a call before you know everything it will ask. Either way, let the breath carry it. The bell holds the time.
Talbiyah. The pilgrim's cry, labbayk, here I am, said from the moment of ihram. Today's word.
Your line: labbayk. Today, when someone calls your name, answer a beat sooner and a little more fully than usual. Here I am. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Pilgrims begin reciting the talbiyah when they enter ihram and repeat it often, men aloud and women more quietly, through the days of the pilgrimage until the stoning on the day of sacrifice, according to the reports of the Prophet's Hajj.

original.note: here I am, at your service: the answer to a call, and the first word of the talbiyah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant pilgrims sing.
what it means: an answer, here I am, to a call, with one God and no partner at its center.
what a scholar hears: the wording Ibn Umar reports in Bukhari, and a call that some readers trace back to Ibrahim in 22:27.
recall: given in place of a fast

'Women's usually lower' and howItsDone 'until the stoning on the day of sacrifice': standard fiqh positions; confirm (Bukhari 1685 on continuing talbiyah until Jamrat al-Aqabah).
